items.q: A 45-year-old patient with acute myeloid leukemia presents with a fever of 38.5°C and an absolute neutrophil count of 300 cells/mm3. They are clinically stable. Which management step is indicated as the priority for this patient?
o: Administer vancomycin as part of initial therapy.
Initiate IV anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam therapy within one hour.
Wait for blood culture results before starting treatment.
Start oral empirical antibiotics immediately.
items.exp: Guidelines mandate starting empirical anti-pseudomonal antibiotics within one hour of triage for febrile neutropenia.
r: Vancomycin is only added for specific indications like hemodynamic instability or suspected catheter infection.
Guidelines mandate starting empirical anti-pseudomonal antibiotics within one hour of triage for febrile neutropenia.
Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring immediate empirical antibiotic administration regardless of culture status.
Oral therapy is reserved only for select patients categorized as low-risk via MASCC scoring.
items.kp: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency requiring initiation of IV anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam antibiotics within one hour of triage.

items.q: A 55-year-old patient receiving chemotherapy develops a fever of 38.2°C sustained for 75 minutes. Their absolute neutrophil count is 400 cells/mm3. MASCC risk scoring yields 23. What is the most appropriate management plan?
o: Initiate outpatient oral therapy with ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate.
Start IV vancomycin plus cefepime immediately.
Delay antibiotic administration until the MASCC score is verified by a specialist.
Admit to the hospital for intravenous meropenem monotherapy.
items.exp: A MASCC score of 21 or more indicates low-risk status suitable for outpatient oral antibiotics.
r: A MASCC score of 21 or more indicates low-risk status suitable for outpatient oral antibiotics.
Vancomycin is not indicated as initial empiric therapy for low-risk, clinically stable febrile neutropenia.
Empirical therapy must be started within one hour; waiting for specialist review is inappropriate.
Outpatient management is appropriate for low-risk patients (MASCC score >= 21) who are clinically stable.
items.kp: MASCC score of 21 or more identifies low-risk febrile neutropenic patients eligible for oral outpatient antibiotic treatment.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient on induction chemotherapy for AML presents with fever (38.5 C) two weeks post-cycle. The patient is currently awaiting CBC results. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Perform a rectal temperature assessment to accurately quantify the severity of the patient's fever.
Wait for absolute neutrophil count results to confirm neutropenia before initiating antibiotics.
Administer prophylactic G-CSF to accelerate marrow recovery before starting antibiotics.
Initiate empirical antibiotics immediately without waiting for the blood count results.
items.exp: Antibiotics are critical in febrile neutropenia and initiation should not be delayed by laboratory turnaround times.
r: Rectal examinations and temperatures are strictly contraindicated in neutropenic patients to prevent bacterial translocation.
Delaying antibiotics in a febrile post-chemotherapy patient is associated with increased morbidity and mortality.
G-CSF is not routinely recommended for the management of already established febrile neutropenia.
Antibiotics are critical in febrile neutropenia and initiation should not be delayed by laboratory turnaround times.
items.kp: Empirical antibiotics should be started immediately for post-chemotherapy fever; diagnostic tests must not delay initial treatment.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient with chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia is currently stable. He has been on levofloxacin prophylaxis for the past two weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy regarding his antimicrobial therapy?
o: Administer a single dose of oral moxifloxacin and observe in the emergency department.
Continue the current fluoroquinolone monotherapy and monitor closely.
Admit the patient for inpatient intravenous empirical antibiotic therapy.
Initiate oral ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate for home management.
items.exp: Oral outpatient therapy is contraindicated for patients already receiving fluoroquinolone prophylaxis per guidelines.
r: Patients on prior fluoroquinolones require hospital admission for IV therapy, not just further oral agents.
Breakthrough fever while on prophylaxis necessitates broader spectrum intravenous therapy.
Oral outpatient therapy is contraindicated for patients already receiving fluoroquinolone prophylaxis per guidelines.
Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis makes the patient ineligible for outpatient oral therapy.
items.kp: Patients currently receiving fluoroquinolone prophylaxis are ineligible for oral outpatient management of febrile neutropenia.

items.q: A 68-year-old patient with known carbapenem-resistant colonization develops clinical instability and septic shock in the intensive care unit. According to ICMR guidelines, which empiric antibiotic regimen should be initiated immediately while awaiting culture results?
o: Meropenem, colistin, vancomycin, and caspofungin
Meropenem, colistin, and vancomycin only
Polymyxin B and piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam and tigecycline
items.exp: Guidelines recommend combining meropenem, colistin or polymyxin B, with a glycopeptide and caspofungin for unstable patients.
r: Guidelines recommend combining meropenem, colistin or polymyxin B, with a glycopeptide and caspofungin for unstable patients.
This regimen lacks the necessary antifungal component recommended by ICMR for critically unstable patients with resistant colonization.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is inappropriate for confirmed carbapenem-resistant isolates, failing the escalation protocol for unstable status.
This combination lacks the broad coverage of polymyxins and antifungal agents required for severe instability in resistant colonization.
items.kp: For patients with known carbapenem-resistant colonization presenting with clinical instability, ICMR recommends escalating to meropenem plus polymyxins, a glycopeptide, and caspofungin.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient with acute myeloid leukemia receives induction chemotherapy and develops febrile neutropenia. After 5 days of appropriate broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy, the patient remains persistently febrile. Neutropenia is projected to persist for another 10 days. Beyond diagnostic imaging, which management step is indicated?
o: Start empiric antiviral therapy for suspected viral reactivation.
Initiate empiric antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B.
Discontinue antibacterial therapy and switch to prophylactic fluconazole.
Continue current antibiotics and observe for another 72 hours.
items.exp: Guidelines mandate empiric antifungal therapy when fever persists despite 4 to 7 days of antibiotics in high-risk patients.
r: Antivirals are not the primary empiric management for persistent fever in prolonged neutropenic high-risk patients.
Guidelines mandate empiric antifungal therapy when fever persists despite 4 to 7 days of antibiotics in high-risk patients.
Fluconazole lacks activity against molds, which are a major concern in prolonged neutropenic fever.
Observation for an additional 72 hours is inappropriate as the neutropenic duration exceeds 7 days.
items.kp: In high-risk neutropenic patients febrile after 4-7 days of antibiotics with expected prolonged neutropenia (>7 days), empiric antifungal therapy is required.
